# Interface Atlas agent guidance

Interface Atlas is an independent frontend UI/UX knowledge library. Do not import Twohearts policies or product assumptions into this repository.

## Reading scope

- Use Atlas when preparing or deliberately revising frontend project design documents, or when the user explicitly requests design review.
- For preparation, start from the brief and catalog/themes.json, then selected theme READMEs. For review, start from the project document and supplied evidence.
- Read detailed theme rules, optional motion/effects, and shared knowledge only when relevant. The knowledge index routes general UI/UX, accessibility/responsive behavior, state, forms, remote outcomes and Agent Experience.
- review-frontend-design is opt-in; review does not automatically run preparation or implement fixes.
- For normal project implementation, prefer that project's self-contained design documents.

## Structure and provenance

- Keep theme folders named for the theme; project suitability belongs in the theme README.
- Keep identity, fit, and limitations in README.md; concrete design rules in design.md.
- Keep source values, referenced concepts, and proposed adaptations distinguishable.
- Preserve creator credits, source URLs, versions or commits, reuse terms, and required notices.
- Unknown reuse terms remain unresolved; a reference link is not permission to copy code or assets.
- Examples illustrate adaptations; they are not universal theme defaults or implemented products.
- Do not mark a theme validated based only on source inspection or color calculations.

## Changes

- Maintain relative links and portable source citations.
- Regenerate the catalog after changing theme discovery metadata; run node tools/catalog.mjs --check.
- Keep shared guidance framework independent. Add adapters only for concrete stack-specific needs.
- Respect the user's authorized scope; routine documentation edits do not require an additional approval process.

# Studio Request — fictional bilingual service trial brief

New trial input, 2026-10-15. This is a design-document exercise, not a request to build or submit to a real service.

A small community studio offers a restrained, approachable service-request web form in English and Vietnamese. Visitors choose a consultation or workshop, give contact details, enter relevant preferences, review answers, and submit one request. The workshop branch asks an additional group-size question; consultation does not. No final data model or field constraints are supplied; label proposed inputs and bounds as project proposals.

Visitors can return from review to change an answer, use step Back and browser Back/Forward, switch interface language while editing, and leave with unsaved work. Changing service can change relevant questions. Preserve understandable review/change context and distinguish final submission from Continue. Support keyboard use, phone-first layout usable on desktop, Light/Dark/System and reduced motion. A full-page flow is acceptable; modal editing is not required.

No backend/API/provider, account system, retention policy, session model, translation pack, real brand assets, font files or implementation stack is supplied. Durable save/resume and remote submission recovery are capability decisions, not established functionality. Distinguish retained draft, remotely accepted request and completed service/appointment. Connections and storage can fail; a lost response can leave an unconfirmed outcome. Do not invent working endpoints, reservations, successful submissions, support channels or authentication requirements.

Propose state ownership, navigation, validation/focus, branch/review, language and uncertain-outcome rules with specific external contract gates. English/Vietnamese translation availability needs a delivery policy; do not assume automatic translation of free-text answers. No payments, AI/agent controls, booking calendar, enrollment, marketing subscriptions or accounts are requested.

Use the unchanged Interface Atlas preparation workflow with relevant revised P0 knowledge. Compare 2–3 candidate READMEs; select one theme and embed its actual rules/tokens. Produce a self-contained design.md, requirement-to-heading evaluation, immutable first draft and contemporaneous reading log, with source creators/versions/terms and performed versus future evidence. No old generated examples, other trials, installed global skills, external web research, UI or runtime implementation are inputs.

# Pocket Practice — fictional consumer trial brief

Status: trial input reconstructed from the delegated brief on 2026-10-15. This is not a request to build a user product.

Pocket Practice is a responsive personal practice web app for independent learners, with a calm, approachable voice. Its English interface may display Vietnamese lesson content. Do not invent a language toggle.

Required tasks: browse and filter a small text-first lesson catalog; bookmark lessons; plan weekly practice; finish a practice with a short note; edit a goal; revisit actual completed work. Data and preferences must survive a reload in the same browser when storage works. There is no account, synchronization, backend, AI, or agent control. Address blocked, full, and malformed storage; distinguish a fresh start from unreadable data and provide useful empty lists. Edits must not disappear silently or claim persistence after a failed write.

Required appearances: Light, Dark, System. Design phone first, usable on desktop, with keyboard and reduced-motion behavior.

Content, brand assets, font files, stack, and a final product data model are not supplied. Mark markup, state ownership, storage formats, conflicts, navigation, Save versus autosave, deletion/undo, and media decisions as project proposals or open contracts. Bound any proposed export/import or recovery facility to actual needs.

Trial procedure: read the required Atlas preparation skill, catalog, two or three candidate theme READMEs, selected theme design and sources, relevant optional motion/effects and only genuinely relevant shared knowledge, plus the project template. Do not read old examples, other trials, all theme details, installed global skills, or web sources. Write only brief.md, design.md, evaluation.md and read-log.json in this staging directory. Produce a self-contained design draft around 2,000–3,000 words, including tokens, pairings, type, geometry, adaptive layout, states, flows, storage/recovery, validation boundaries and precise provenance. Do not implement or claim rendered proof or production guarantees.

Repository supplied revision: 782159e8e2510933c76989ff9fd9546d282c62cd.

# Form & Field — trial brief

Fictional project: an independent homeware studio's image-led responsive webstore with roughly 50 products. English interface; display money in USD. The brand should feel calm and design-led while purchase actions stay clear.

Required guest tasks: browse the collection; search and filter; inspect accurate product images; choose an available color/size variant and quantity; add products to a cart; edit quantities and remove lines; review authoritative prices, availability, and totals; hand off to hosted checkout. A cart draft must survive same-browser reload when storage works. The backend will own authoritative prices, stock, quote totals, and checkout. Connection and browser storage can fail; prices and availability can change; unknown checkout outcomes require truthful recovery.

No API, payment provider, stock-reservation contract, tax rules, real product catalog, product media, rights records, brand assets, font files, or implementation stack is supplied. Do not invent working endpoints, reservation timers, successful orders, legal guarantees, or a chosen provider. Propose handoff boundaries and identify unresolved contract gates. No account, wishlist, AI/agent, or loyalty flows are requested. Do not represent Gallery's generated illustration fixtures as real product photographs.

Support Light, Dark, and System; start with a phone-first layout usable on desktop. Include keyboard operation and reduced-motion behavior. Treat additional design decisions as project proposals or open questions.

This trial uses the existing Interface Atlas prepare-frontend-design workflow at repository snapshot `782159e8e2510933c76989ff9fd9546d282c62cd`. Select from the catalog, review 2–3 candidate READMEs, and load only selected detailed rules, provenance, relevant motion, and the template. No other trial, old project example, installed global skill, outside web source, asset binary, implementation, or repository mutation is part of this exercise.

Deliver a self-contained draft `design.md` of roughly 2,000–3,000 words as needed, an `evaluation.md` that maps requirements to exact headings and separates Atlas guidance from project proposals and blocked backend work, and a contemporaneous `read-log.json` of every repository content read with first-read order, purpose, UTF-8 bytes, and SHA-256. No UI, usability, actual model-token, or billing measurement is claimed.

# Shared knowledge

Use this index to select guidance for preparing or explicitly reviewing a project's design. Start from the brief or a concrete review question. Read applicable sections and their dependencies/credits; do not load every chapter, source registry or upstream skill bundle. Routine implementation normally uses the project's self-contained documents.

| Chapter | Select when there is a decision about | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [General UI/UX design](ui-ux-design.md) | User goals, task/content structure, journeys, hierarchy, layout, typography, semantic color, UX writing, component mapping or validation questions | Cross-theme planning/review; use relevant sections for unresolved decisions |
| [Design reference evaluation](design-reference-evaluation.md) | A chosen external reference or a consequential theme-fit choice that remains unresolved | Use only the relevant reference check or equivalent-task comparison; no default source survey |
| [Accessibility and responsive behavior](accessibility-and-responsive.md) | Names/semantics, keyboard/focus, errors/status, zoom/reflow, content order, touch/input differences, language/RTL, chosen motion or appearance checks | Task-scoped decisions and evidence; not a conformance certificate |
| [State ownership and durable recovery](state-and-recovery.md) | Drafts/records, persistence, reload recovery, concurrent edits, migration, reset or import/export | P0 knowledge draft; select actual state capabilities |
| [Forms and navigation](forms-and-navigation.md) | Editable inputs, validation, modal editing, branching/review, dirty exit, Back/Forward or save/resume | P0 knowledge draft; choose relevant flow sections |
| [Uncertain outcomes](uncertain-outcomes.md) | Remote effects, lost replies, repeat submission, retry, cancellation or reconciliation | P0 knowledge draft; requires project/service facts and gates |
| [Agent Experience](agent-experience.md) | Human-facing agent work, proposals, progress, intervention or control | Lifecycle principles and contract questions; no agent runtime implementation |

Theme identity, values, effects and motion remain in the chosen theme package. Shared guides resolve cross-theme decisions. Select by feature: a static portfolio need not load persistence or remote outcomes; a local practice app should not acquire agent/backend flows; a remote branching form may need all three P0 chapters. An existing resolved design can need only one relevant section for a narrow revision.

Reference evaluation is conditional on a selected outside source or unresolved theme fit. Use component translation only when the mapping needs resolution, and the motion contract only when motion is chosen and not already resolved. Do not automatically create a specimen, introduce a runtime, fetch external sources or reread a source collection. Resolve accepted decisions into the project handoff.

Turn selected guidance into explicit project values, behaviors and open contracts in design.md. Do not make the consuming project repeatedly load Atlas. Separate observations, inherited design rules, new proposals and unsupported capabilities. Source inspection, heuristic review, browser checks, assistive-technology checks and user research are different evidence.

The P0 drafts retain their [source ledger](../references/p0-research.md), [earlier review](../references/p0-review.md), and [trial history](../examples/p0-evaluation/README.md). They are now routed by the updated preparation and opt-in review workflows; their draft status does not imply production behavior was validated. [Skill adaptation credits](../references/skill-adaptations.md), including the [reference and craft additions](../references/skill-adaptations.md#2026-10-20-reference-and-craft-additions), record creator/license mappings and retained notices. The [research comparison](../references/skill-research.md) is optional background, not a required skill read.

# Focused accessibility and responsive decisions

Status: adaptation draft, updated 2026-10-20. Original Atlas synthesis by **Tamir (Phi Vuong Tuong Tam), with Codex AI assistance**. These are conditional planning and review questions, not normative requirements or a conformance assessment. No interface testing is claimed.

## Select the relevant questions

Load when a task depends on interactive controls, assistive technology, resizing/zoom, translated content, touch, or motion/media. Select affected surfaces and states; skip absent features. This does not trigger an audit of every route or domain. A project claiming a standard must establish applicable criteria and authoritative sources separately; upstream skill checklists do not establish obligations.

Record supported environments and unresolved coverage: browsers, inputs, viewport/content constraints, languages/direction, and relevant assistive technology. Choose checks for task risk. Mockups cannot prove keyboard or screen-reader behavior.

## Controls, meaning, and focus

For an interactive task, ask:

- Which native elements or existing accessible components fit the action? If custom behavior is necessary, who owns its keyboard model and states?
- Can people identify actions from visible labels and accessible names? Do icons, instructions, field groups, headings, and relationships convey information the task needs?
- Can people complete the task with supported inputs? Can keyboard users locate their position, reach required actions, and leave temporary UI? Do hover, dragging, or gestures need an alternative?
- When a dialog opens, an error appears, or navigation completes, where should attention and focus go? Can the person return to a sensible location without losing context?

Plan behavior, then inspect implementation. Source can reveal missing associations or suspicious focus rules; it does not establish what a browser and assistive-technology combination announces. Extra ARIA is not itself evidence of improvement.

[Forms and navigation](forms-and-navigation.md) owns field errors, validation timing, dialog editing, dirty exit, route focus, and resume. [State and recovery](state-and-recovery.md) owns retained drafts and save acknowledgement; [uncertain outcomes](uncertain-outcomes.md) owns feedback when remote completion is unknown. Use the relevant contract when it exists; accessible wording must communicate actual capabilities.

## Adaptation with real content

When a task spans constrained sizes or changing text, ask:

- At what content pressure does the structure stop working? What should wrap, stack, collapse, scroll, or move to detail while preserving the task and reading order?
- Can people find required content and controls at supported narrow sizes, zoom/text settings, and orientation? Do sticky regions, overlays, browser chrome, or the onscreen keyboard cover an action or focused content?
- What happens to long names, identifiers, translated labels, multiline errors, empty data, and large values? If abbreviated, how can someone obtain the full value with their input method?
- If multiple languages or directions are supported, do layout, controls, labels, and mixed-direction values read correctly? Which elements intentionally keep a physical direction?

Choose breakpoints from observed content needs and supported conditions, then record transitions. Atlas sets no shared device list, spacing scale, font floor, or framework. Preserve information relationships when changing presentation.

## Perception, status, and optional media

Can people distinguish actions, selections, errors, and status without depending on one visual cue? Which foreground/background pairs actually render, including overlays, images, opacity, and theme modes? Record measured pairs and the project's applicable target; do not guess contrast ratios.

When motion exists, what information or control remains if it is reduced, interrupted, or absent? Does media need text alternatives, captions, or playback controls for this task? Can important feedback be found after a transient message disappears? Keep chosen color, type, and motion values with theme and project decisions.

## Record the chosen motion contract

When motion is chosen, resolve the applicable theme rules into one short project record: purpose and owning component; trigger and static equivalent; repeat, interruption and exit behavior; preference precedence; and performed versus pending checks. Omit a second record if the governing project document already resolves these points.

Name unresolved implementation mappings. A library's reduced-motion option may retain effects that the project makes immediate; inspect the installed version and actual behavior against the chosen policy. Logical completion, accepted actions and necessary focus transfer stay in their existing owners, independent of presentation callbacks.

Use existing CSS when it supports the required behavior. A runtime needs a concrete reason, such as interrupted gestures, presence or shared layout. Record the installed version when relevant. Timings and easing remain theme/project choices; property selection alone is not performance evidence.

Check the selected path, including relevant repeat/reversal, live preference changes and departure during movement. Preserve content and useful controls when presentation is absent or interrupted. Report the exercised environment and limits; source inspection does not establish frame performance or accessibility.

Method credits: existing Atlas [Editorial](../themes/editorial/motion.md)/[Pulse](../themes/pulse/motion.md) proposals, and linked technical guidance from **Matt Perry / Motion team and contributors**, [AI-kit skill](https://github.com/motiondivision/ai-kit/blob/8dc4f7a375f7f5cc32df1aa679b5d19c463651b4/plugins/motion/skills/motion/SKILL.md) at `8dc4f7a375f7f5cc32df1aa679b5d19c463651b4`. AI-kit metadata declares MIT, but a complete notice was not found in the inspected tree. This is original synthesis and references, not redistribution of the upstream skill bundle. The separate core-library license does not resolve that notice gap. See the [inspected source paths and adaptation boundary](../references/skill-adaptations.md#2026-10-20-reference-and-craft-additions).

## Report evidence at its actual level

Distinguish **planned**, **source inspected**, **rendered/interaction observed**, **measured**, and **not checked**. Name surface/state, content sample, environment, action or command, result, and limits. A screenshot can show clipping at one size; it cannot prove keyboard reachability. An accessibility tree exposes computed names/roles; a screen-reader walkthrough checks another layer. Automated findings need interpretation, and a clean run does not establish task usability or conformance.

Report observed barriers and consequences; otherwise record open questions or recommendations. Prefer focused corrections in the existing system. Repeat affected interaction and adaptation checks after changes. Explicitly exclude uninspected routes, states, devices, and assistive technologies from conclusions.

## Method credits

# Agent Experience

Use this guidance when a project exposes agent work to an operator. Adapt it to the execution service's actual capabilities.

## Make activity understandable

Show the objective, current observed activity, relevant evidence, outputs, and available controls. Distinguish agent explanations from confirmed tool results. Present progress measurements only when they are known.

Keep execution state, requests for user attention, pending control commands, and connection freshness distinguishable. Losing an event stream does not establish that execution failed.

## Preserve operator control

Offer input, correction, dismissal, or execution controls where the service supports them. Show their scope and pending outcome. Do not present an accepted command as a completed operation.

A decision request should identify the exact proposal being decided. If it changes, the interface needs a decision on the changed proposal. Show action results separately from the decision.

A retry should explain known prior effects and remaining uncertainty. Avoid implying that repeating work is harmless when completion is unknown.

## Resolve project control questions

For a proposed or existing agent control surface, decide which of these questions actually applies:

- What can the agent suggest, change or execute, and who may authorize each effect? Show the actual target, scope, material consequences and supporting evidence before a decision.
- Which immutable proposal identity/version and request revision bind that decision? Editing scope, changed upstream data or expiry needs a defined revalidation/review path; a decision on an old proposal is not unlimited permission.
- Can the operator reject, edit, pause, cancel or reverse the effect? Name supported controls and their limits. Keep a local editing choice, submitted decision, accepted command and confirmed execution result distinct.
- What survives interruption or reload, and how can the original action be discovered? Route unknown results, overlapping changed intent and stale observations through the project's documented service contract. Gate action enablement on missing recovery/authority capabilities instead of inventing guarantees.
- What helps someone inspect evidence, steer work, understand uncertainty and resume? Do not fabricate confidence percentages, progress estimates or an approval-volume budget.

Use [forms/navigation](forms-and-navigation.md) for editable decisions and focus, [state/recovery](state-and-recovery.md) for retained local intent, and [uncertain outcomes](uncertain-outcomes.md) for remote controls and observation. Read only the applicable sections. These are design questions, not a policy engine or production control contract.

## Keep attention stable

Preserve focus, selection, and reading position during updates. Make new events discoverable without automatically moving the operator's context. Important decisions and failures remain available after temporary notifications disappear.

# Evaluate design references

Status: adaptation draft, 2026-10-20. Original Atlas synthesis by **Tamir (Phi Vuong Tuong Tam), with Codex AI assistance**. No product validation is claimed.

Read for a chosen external reference or an unresolved visual-direction decision. Existing Atlas themes and resolved project rules do not require another source survey. Carry accepted decisions into the project's self-contained design document.

## Evaluate the selected contribution

Name the decision and the source contribution: grouping, a type relationship, component behavior or a visual technique. Inspect the relevant material and enough context to interpret it. Reuse the existing provenance record for creator, URL, inspected revision/date and reuse terms; do not create a second ledger or reread content solely to fingerprint it.

Trace the proposed rule through the source's description, tokens and examples. Check contradictions, omitted consequential states and unsupported claims such as “accessible” or “production ready.” A dependency's notice does not establish the reuse terms of the source's prose, fonts, imagery or code. Keep unresolved artifacts as reference links rather than bundling them.

Retain, adapt or reject the idea against the approved project contract and chosen theme. State the reason for an exception. Resolve accepted ideas into actual project values, content order, applicable states and behavior. Source preferences do not silently override user choices or capability boundaries. Identify performed checks and pending questions at their actual evidence level.

## Compare candidates on equivalent work

Use a comparison only when theme fit remains consequentially unresolved. Preserve an explicit user selection. Start with candidate READMEs; inspect detailed rules only for plausible candidates. Two can be sufficient.

Choose a representative task and surface. Hold decision content, labels, data, available actions and meaningful states equivalent. Include relevant content pressure, such as a long title, missing image or validation message. Use original or owner-provided content with known rights; better imagery or shorter copy must not give one candidate an artificial advantage.

Let hierarchy, typography and composition express each theme. Compare action recognition, information grouping, readability, state interpretation, adaptation needs and supported contexts. Record task, constants, differences, tradeoffs, evidence type and selection or uncertainty. A document sketch is desk reasoning; rendered checks and observations of users are separate evidence. Do not invent a numerical usability score. When task differences are immaterial, use the brief and owner preference to resolve the aesthetic choice.

# Forms and navigation

Status: P0 research draft for review, revision 0.2-draft, 2026-10-15. Original Atlas synthesis by Tamir (Phi Vuong Tuong Tam), with Codex AI assistance. External authors are credited references, not endorsers. No source code, assets, or wholesale pattern text is incorporated.

## When to load this chapter

Load when a design involves editable input, validation, modal editing, multiple steps, review/change loops, unsaved work, navigation restoration, or interrupted sessions. A local calculator or browser-only journal can need these decisions without a backend. Consult [state and recovery](state-and-recovery.md) only when state ownership or persistence matters; consult [uncertain outcomes](uncertain-outcomes.md#safe-retry-and-recovery) when a remote action may have taken effect without a confirmed response. A spinner alone does not establish that condition.

**Evidence boundary.** WCAG success criteria are normative requirements at their stated conformance levels. Understanding documents explain them; WAI tutorials and APG offer informative implementation guidance. GOV.UK describes tested government-service conventions whose applicability to another product needs judgment. The decisions marked **Atlas proposal** below are original synthesis, not standards requirements. [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/2024/REC-WCAG22-20241212/), [Understanding documentation](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html), and [APG introduction](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/about/introduction/).

## Inputs and validation timing

WAI recommends labels associated with controls, using native HTML labels where possible. The visible label, accessible name, hint, requiredness, and error serve different purposes. An accessible name alone does not supply instructions visible to everyone; WCAG 3.3.2 also applies to optional fields. [WAI labels](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/labels/), [Understanding 3.3.2](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/labels-or-instructions.html).

**Atlas proposal:** Record each input's accepted meaning, required/optional status, format examples, bounds, normalization, grouping, and available control semantics. Keep a persistent visible label as the usual choice; placeholder content can add an example. State why a constrained format is necessary. Preserve entered text through correction, and explain any consequential transformation. Do not use numeric semantics merely because an identifier contains digits.

WAI advises accommodating reasonable input formats and distinguishes convenient client validation from security at a server boundary. For a form that sends data to a server, client checks alone cannot protect that boundary. This does not require adding a server to a client-only tool. [WAI validation](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/validation/).

**Atlas proposal:** Choose validation timing by error cost. Validate a submitted step before advancing; allow incomplete drafts to remain editable. Validate during typing only when feedback is useful immediately, such as a visible length limit, without treating every intermediate value as an error. If checking on blur, avoid stealing focus or producing an error before a meaningful attempt. After an error, define when correction clears it. Distinguish syntax checks, cross-field rules, and remote eligibility checks; a remote check's pending or unavailable result is not proof that the input is wrong. If input changes while a check runs, the result must correspond to the current value before it is shown as authoritative.

## Validation and error recovery

WCAG 3.3.1 requires an automatically detected input error to identify the affected item and describe the error in text. WAI describes both overall and field-level feedback, including a linked error list and programmatic relationships between a field and its message. [Understanding 3.3.1](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-identification.html), [WAI notification](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/notifications/).

**Atlas proposal:** A failed submission retains the user's values, selection where feasible, and a path to correction. Describe the problem and the accepted next action near the field; do not rely on a red border. Associate the message with the control, expose invalid state appropriately, and remove stale associations when corrected. For several errors, a summary can explain the failed attempt and link to exact controls or a meaningful first control in a group. Match summary and inline wording.

GOV.UK requires a focused summary for every validation failure in its system. Atlas treats that as a strong comparative pattern, not a universal WCAG requirement: a small inline edit may use one associated message and a documented focus target. If using a summary, move focus after the failed attempt, keep it visible, and make its links work with keyboard and zoom. Choose between focused feedback and live announcements deliberately; test for repeated or missing speech. [GOV.UK error summary](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/error-summary/).

An unavailable service, lost permission, storage failure, and unknown remote outcome need their own recovery text. They should not mark a correct field invalid. Where relevant, retain the draft and resolve the action under the appropriate state or outcome contract.

HTML interactive validation can stop submission before the submit event; the browser may report and focus an invalid control. [HTML constraint validation](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#constraint-validation), [submission algorithm](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#form-submission-algorithm).

**Atlas proposal:** choose the owner of interactive validation feedback and focus. A native-feedback path must account for invalid events and browser behavior. A custom-feedback path must arrange for its full error collection, associations and summary to run without competing native feedback; defining it only in a submit handler is insufficient when native validation blocks that event. Record whether/how native interactive validation is suppressed while retaining useful input semantics and server checks. Do not prescribe novalidate universally. Cover the submit button, Enter/implicit submission, scripted entry points and inactive branch controls under the same decision.

## Pending actions and available controls

WCAG 4.1.3 addresses status messages that can be presented by assistive technology without moving focus. Its scope does not turn every new content region into a live announcement. [Understanding 4.1.3](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html).

**Atlas proposal:** For an ordinary pending save, keep the editing context stable, show a truthful status, prevent duplicate activation at the action boundary, and define what remains editable. Preserve a useful focus destination through success and failure. A failure should leave a persistent explanation and reachable recovery action; background completion should not pull focus away from unrelated work. If the action explicitly navigates or opens a dialog, specify that new context separately. If editing remains available, bind completion to the submitted candidate: success for A cannot clear later edit B, replace B, or automatically close its editor. Define the dirty baseline and completion ordering using [save snapshots](state-and-recovery.md#save-snapshots-and-completion). For remote ambiguity, use the [outcome distinctions](uncertain-outcomes.md#outcome-states-and-copy).

Native `disabled` controls leave the tab sequence; disabled form controls are excluded from constraint validation and the form submission entry list. `aria-disabled` conveys unavailability but requires application behavior to suppress activation. It can retain discoverability and focus. APG discusses this tradeoff rather than prescribing one choice everywhere. [HTML disabled controls and submission](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/form-control-infrastructure.html#enabling-and-disabling-form-controls:-the-disabled-attribute), [ARIA disabled state](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#aria-disabled), [APG keyboard guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/keyboard-interface/#kbd_disabled_controls).

**Atlas proposal:** Choose per control. A temporarily unavailable pending action may stay focusable with guarded `aria-disabled`; cover keyboard, pointer, implicit form submission, and alternate action entry points. Native disabling may suit an unavailable field, but record its effect on focus and submitted values. Put the reason nearby. Never promise that styling or an ARIA attribute alone blocks the operation, and avoid disabling an entire form when users still need to read or correct it.

## Modal editing and dirty exit

APG's modal pattern places focus inside, contains Tab navigation, provides an accessible name and visible closing control, closes with Escape, and ordinarily returns focus to the invoker or a logical workflow destination. Native HTML `dialog` provides modal showing and focus behavior, but initial focus still needs deliberate selection. Native close requests and unconditional closing are different paths. [APG modal dialog](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/), [HTML dialog](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interactive-elements.html#the-dialog-element).

**Atlas proposal — same-dialog dirty confirmation:** For a bounded editor whose work would be lost, clean Cancel/Escape closes directly. A dirty close request changes the contents of the existing named dialog to a confirmation state. Keep the draft in memory, make editor controls temporarily inactive, and focus **Keep editing**. That action, or Escape in this confirmation state, restores the editor and its last usable editing focus; **Discard changes** closes and returns focus logically. Do not show a second stacked dialog for this proposal. Define backdrop and close-button behavior consistently with the same close request.

This Escape sequence is an explicit Atlas adaptation: it differs from immediate close in APG and needs evaluation for comprehension. It is not a claim that native dialog cancellation can always be prevented. Specify handling for native cancel/close events, forced closure, missing opener, pending saves, and a full-page alternative when modality cannot be supported. A dialog close is not evidence of save success or remote cancellation. Re-authentication and unknown pending work require separate decisions.

## Multi-step and branching forms

WAI recommends logical step groups, recognizable optional stages, recurring instructions, and understandable progress. WCAG 3.3.7 covers repeated information in the same process, subject to its exceptions; its Understanding document explicitly does not require storing answers between sessions. Changing a control value must not unexpectedly change context without advance advice under 3.2.2. [WAI multi-page forms](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/multi-page/), [Understanding 3.3.7](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/redundant-entry.html), [Understanding 3.2.2](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/on-input.html).

**Atlas proposal:** Model steps as a flow with named destinations and branch conditions, not merely a counter. Define what constitutes a draft versus a valid step, what Back preserves, and whether jumping ahead is allowed. Report exact totals only when the route is known; conditional questions may change them. If an earlier answer makes later answers irrelevant, decide whether to retain them as inactive draft or clear them with explanation. Exclude irrelevant answers from final review/submission, and revalidate dependent answers when the branch changes. A hidden field must not become an unreachable blocker.

GOV.UK's check-answers pattern pre-populates edited answers, returns users directly to review, and asks newly required questions before returning when an edit changes the journey. This is useful comparative service guidance. [GOV.UK check answers](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/check-answers/).

**Atlas proposal:** Preserve a review-return destination when entering an editor. After a valid edit, restore review near the changed section with a logical focus target; disclose new omissions or changed consequences. Keep a clear final action separate from intermediate Continue. Select review, correction, reversibility, or confirmation in proportion to consequences. WCAG 3.3.4 offers alternative safeguards for its stated legal, financial, data, and test-response scope; it does not require a confirmation dialog on every save. [Understanding 3.3.4](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/error-prevention-legal-financial-data.html).

## Navigation, focus, and scroll

GOV.UK's Back component returns to the actual previous page in its prior state. Browser history is a separate navigation surface: HTML defines Back/Forward traversal and automatic/manual scroll restoration. Focus order must preserve meaning and operation, but WCAG does not select a universal SPA router or one focus target for every route. [GOV.UK Back](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/back-link/), [HTML history](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/nav-history-apis.html#the-history-interface), [Understanding 2.4.3](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-order.html).

**Atlas proposal:** Specify full document loads, client transitions, fragments, review-return links, and history traversal separately. For a new logical page, choose a meaningful title, destination heading/main region or other justified focus target, scroll position, and loading/failure behavior. For Back/Forward, choose how form answers, filters, selected records, scroll, and focus are restored without fighting the browser's restoration. Preserve fragments and deep-link destinations. If an old target disappeared, choose the nearest logical context. A failed route must provide a reachable recovery path rather than leaving focus on removed content. Avoid creating duplicate history entries or rewriting traversal merely to imitate a prescribed workflow. These are project contracts to implement and test, not browser behavior demonstrated by this document.

## Unsaved work, resume, and expiry

An in-app dirty-navigation decision can show product-specific consequences. Browser-level unload prompts have platform restrictions, including activation conditions and browser-chosen wording. Chrome's lifecycle guidance warns that termination events cannot reliably protect data, particularly on mobile, and recommends attaching `beforeunload` only while unsaved work exists. [HTML unload checks](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/browsing-the-web.html#check-if-unloading-is-canceled), [Chrome lifecycle guidance](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/page-lifecycle-api#the-beforeunload-event).

**Atlas proposal:** Define dirty state and the transitions that risk actual loss. Explain what leaving loses; offer continue editing, discard, or a supported save. Account for reload, tab close, external links, and browser traversal without promising interception. Treat an unload prompt as additional protection. Durable draft mechanics belong in [state and recovery](state-and-recovery.md), with the product's real limits.

Save/resume is a capability decision: identify what is retained, for how long, where resumption works, how it is found, and which sensitive answers are excluded. An explicit save needs evidence before claiming completion. Session authentication expiry and draft lifetime are separate; after re-authentication, disclose what can actually be restored. For content-imposed time limits, evaluate WCAG 2.2.1's turn-off, adjustment, extension, and exception provisions rather than assuming security removes all obligations. [Understanding 2.2.1](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/timing-adjustable.html).

## Bounded review scenarios and remaining evidence

Desk-review these proposed paths: (1) submit two errors, correct one, follow the remaining summary link; (2) edit while a check is pending and receive an obsolete result; (3) request dirty close, Keep editing/Escape, then discard; (4) change a branch from review and answer the new required question; (5) go Back/Forward to a long step with restored answers and scroll; (6) encounter session expiry with both a saved draft and later unsaved edits; (7) submit an invalid native-constrained form through a button and Enter under the chosen feedback/focus policy; (8) save A, edit B while pending, then receive A success or failure without losing B. Trace the intended state, visible text, available actions, focus, and loss boundary. These are coverage questions, not executed acceptance results.

No application, fixture, router, persistence layer, browser interaction, keyboard run, screen-reader run, zoom test, mobile lifecycle experiment, or usability study was executed. # State ownership and durable recovery

Status: researched draft for review, revision 0.2-draft, 2026-10-15. Atlas synthesis by **Tamir (Phi Vuong Tuong Tam), with Codex AI assistance**. The decision rules below are Atlas proposals; attributed platform facts describe the inspected sources. No interface, storage experiment, migration, or recovery flow has been implemented or behaviorally validated.

## Read triggers and boundaries

Read when a brief includes reload recovery, offline work, saved preferences, personal records, imports, undo, multiple tabs, or local drafts of remotely owned objects. Skip detailed storage decisions for disposable presentation state whose loss has no material consequence. Load [forms and navigation](forms-and-navigation.md) or [uncertain outcomes](uncertain-outcomes.md) when leaving an editor or submitting a remote action also matters.

This chapter helps choose a contract. It does not require IndexedDB, a backend, accounts, or export controls in every project. A small preference and an irreplaceable practice history justify different investment. A theme's visual rules cannot determine either contract.

## Ownership and lifetime

**Atlas proposal:** identify the authority for each fact before choosing storage. Authority means the value a particular decision must consult; it need not be the location currently rendering that value. Name who can change it and the boundary across which it must survive.

| State | Possible owner and lifetime | Project decision required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Search, open panel, selection | Page memory or shareable URL | Should Back, reload, or a copied link restore it? |
| Unsubmitted editor draft | User intent in memory or a draft store | Save boundary, dirty comparison, retention, discard and recovery |
| Local personal records | Validated browser store, if product chooses local authority | Acknowledgement, capacity, conflict, backup and deletion policy |
| Remote record and editable draft | Service owns committed value; editor owns proposed changes | Base revision, acceptance, stale edits and reconciliation |
| Cached catalog or derived total | Rebuildable observation with freshness limits | When to invalidate; which decisions require current authority |
| Cart and purchase attempt | Browser may own intended items; service owns commercial outcome | Keep cart revision and recoverable attempt identity distinct |

An updated screen is not evidence that a write succeeded. Describe draft, pending write, acknowledged value, failed write, conflicting value and unknown remote outcome separately. Optimistic display is permissible when its rollback, pending indication and retry semantics are explicit. Avoid making every local preference show a save dialog; scale interaction to loss and consequence.

If Undo is offered, specify the inverse operation, affected records, expiry boundaries, interaction with later edits and save-failure behavior. A transient undo slot needs explicit navigation/reload semantics. Restoring browser cart intent cannot restore a remote price, stock reservation or purchase status. The storefront trial's latest-removal slot is one project proposal, not a universal pattern.

## Acknowledgement is not retention

**Verified platform facts:** IndexedDB commits transaction changes together; request success does not establish transaction completion. Durability is a hint: `strict` asks the user agent to verify persistent-medium writing; `relaxed` permits operating-system acknowledgement; `default` delegates. [W3C Indexed Database API 3.0, §§2.7 and 5.4](https://www.w3.org/TR/2025/WD-IndexedDB-3-20250813/).

Google documents Chrome's move to relaxed default durability from Chrome 121, explains the completion/OS-buffer distinction, and cautions that selecting strict durability does not eliminate data loss. [Thomas Steiner, Chrome for Developers](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/indexeddb-durability-mode-now-defaults-to-relaxed).

**Atlas proposal:** if using IndexedDB, only acknowledge the intended local save after the transaction completes successfully. Keep a draft on failure. Choose a durability hint for the actual risk/performance tradeoff and supported browsers; do not turn `strict` into a universal requirement. A local acknowledgement says neither “synced” nor “order completed.” Multiple browser stores and remote requests do not become one transaction because the interface has one Save button.

The Storage Standard starts local buckets in best-effort mode. Persistence requires permission; persistent storage is protected from automatic clearing without origin/user involvement. Usage and quota are estimates. [WHATWG Storage Standard, §§4.5–7](https://storage.spec.whatwg.org/). WebKit documents quota failures, eviction under storage pressure or inactivity, and heuristics for granting persistence. Its quoted quota is an upper bound, not allocated free space. [Sihui Liu, Updates to Storage Policy](https://webkit.org/blog/14403/updates-to-storage-policy/).

**Atlas proposal:** specify expected same-browser reload recovery while storage remains available, and disclose material limits. Persistence requests may improve protection; design denial and unavailability paths. Request at a meaningful saving moment if justified; Google's guidance discourages unexplained page-load requests and immediate repeated prompts. [Pete LePage, Persistent storage](https://web.dev/articles/persistent-storage). User clearing, browser/profile removal and device loss still require a separate recovery strategy when the product promises recoverability. A second copy in the same browser eviction boundary is not an independent backup.

## Save snapshots and completion

**Atlas proposal:** bind each save to an immutable candidate, its draft version and authoritative base revision. If save A is pending while the user edits B, A's success acknowledges A only. B remains dirty; do not replace it, clear its dirty flag, close its editor or navigate away as though B was saved. Define whether saves are serialized, coalesced before dispatch or allowed to overlap, and how older completions are prevented from replacing newer acknowledged state. Failure preserves the latest draft and identifies which candidate failed. An acknowledgement from an invalidated store generation cannot clean a current draft.

This is a proposed product invariant. IndexedDB stores record values by value, so changing an in-memory object later does not update its stored record. [Indexed Database API 3.0, §2.3](https://www.w3.org/TR/2025/WD-IndexedDB-3-20250813/#values). The project's dirty baseline tracks acknowledged content, rather than the last click, current input or a generic success flag. Explicitly disabling editing while saving is another project option when its interaction consequences are acceptable.

## Concurrent edits

**Source guidance and platform facts:** WHATWG's informative Web storage introduction warns authors to assume no `localStorage` locking across relevant browser contexts. Its read/increment/write example can race. Normative API definitions include `SecurityError` for access and `QuotaExceededError` for a failed write. [HTML Standard, Web storage](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webstorage.html). IndexedDB prevents concurrent modification of stores within an overlapping read/write transaction's scope. [Indexed Database API 3.0, §2.7.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/2025/WD-IndexedDB-3-20250813/).

**Atlas proposal:** choose explicitly among disposable last-writer-wins, restricted editing, reviewed replacement, or a concrete conflict-safe mechanism appropriate to the product. A local revision field alone is insufficient. Reading a revision and later writing localStorage leaves an intervening-write window; a storage event or broadcast can notify but does not close it. A timestamp is not a lock.

For an IndexedDB revision-check pattern, read the current revision, compare the draft's base, validate and write the next value/revision inside the same appropriately scoped read/write transaction. Include all records whose consistency matters. Do not describe a separate read transaction followed by an unconditional write as equivalent. Keep user review/network waits outside the transaction, then recheck; another conflict can occur during review. Determine whether a rejected draft can be merged by field, reapplied as a named operation, or requires replacement review. Blindly replaying an entire stale snapshot can erase unrelated changes.

Pocket Practice proposes this transactional revision pattern, but still lacks exact reapplication semantics. Form & Field's localStorage revision plus other-tab review proposal leaves the write race unresolved. These are document-level implementation gates from the [consumer](../examples/coverage-evaluation/consumer-app/design.md) and [storefront](../examples/coverage-evaluation/storefront/design.md) trials, not observed failures or proof of correctness.

## Read failure, migration and reset

**Atlas proposal:** startup must distinguish loading, validated existing data, absent record, unavailable access, malformed/invalid data and unsupported schema. Absence does not prove first-ever use: data may previously have been removed. Default values may be usable without asserting that the user never created anything.

On a read error, avoid automatic writes to the affected authority. Preserve readable original bytes/records where possible; do not overwrite them with empty defaults on the next ordinary edit. A temporary in-memory draft must be clearly labeled and guarded against autosave replacement. Retry, inspect/export safely where feasible, migrate a supported version, and informed reset are distinct actions. Do not label every access failure “corruption” or promise that unreadable content can always be exported.

For migration, state recognized source/target versions, validation rules, interruption behavior, concurrent old-client behavior and rollback/recovery route. Preserve the original until the replacement has met the chosen completion/durability checks; staging and copying require their own quota budget. Database version upgrades and application payload schema versions are separate concerns. IndexedDB upgrades may be blocked by open connections; requesting a lower database version fails. [Indexed Database API 3.0, §4.3](https://www.w3.org/TR/2025/WD-IndexedDB-3-20250813/). Treat blocked upgrade, denial, quota exhaustion and unknown schema as different recovery paths. Never silently downgrade or delete a newer unknown version.

Reset must identify what will be discarded, offer available backup/review, and state whether the temporary draft replaces the saved record. If reset writing fails, retain the guarded draft and explain the remaining state. Do not claim recovery succeeded because a confirmation dialog closed. Form & Field's reviewed quarantine rule fixes a useful counterexample: “start empty after parse failure” alone allowed the next cart edit to destroy unreadable prior intent.

## Replacement and stale writers

**Atlas proposal:** deletion, reset, replacement import and migration must define what happens to queued autosaves, in-flight completions, old tabs and recovered drafts. A successful replacement does not prevent a later stale write from resurrecting deleted data or overwriting restored state. Retire obsolete work at an enforceable authority boundary: for example, transactionally check a non-reused store generation plus revision, or use verified writer exclusion with an explicit reconciliation policy. A UI flag, a storage notification, or resetting a counter to an earlier value is insufficient for a claimed conflict-safe replacement.

Record when obsolete work is rejected, what happens if replacement fails, and how an older client or draft learns that its base no longer exists. Do not silently reapply it. Preserve a separately named draft for review where appropriate. The mechanism remains a project choice; every write path must participate in its checks. A separate confirmation screen or a transactional import alone does not provide that guarantee.

## Backups and capacity

**Atlas proposal:** decide whether local loss is acceptable, whether an independent service copy exists, or whether export/import is warranted. Define data sensitivity, retention and who controls recovery copies. Browser storage is not itself an access-control or secrecy guarantee. Imported data requires schema validation and safe rendering; parsing JSON does not establish semantic validity.

When export/import is offered, use one explicit envelope for creation, updates, temporary-mode edits, migration and recovery. Every state the product permits users to create must have an export representation accepted by the compatible importer, including identifiers, history, Unicode content and required metadata. This is a format/capacity design invariant; actual destination writes can still fail because browser resources differ. Resolve growth at capacity before enabling indefinite accumulation. Do not silently evict user history to make a save appear successful.

Specify export version, scope, omitted data, integrity checks, supported historical versions and replacement/merge behavior. Preview import consequences and validate the full candidate before replacement; commit within an identified boundary, preserving prior authority on failure. A successful file selection is not a successful restore. A raw diagnostic export of unreadable content must not claim to be a valid backup. If file completion cannot be observed, describe the export action truthfully rather than claiming an independently verified backup.

Pocket Practice's initial import-only size/count caps could reject history that ordinary use was allowed to accumulate. Its reviewed draft replaces those caps with a shared capacity gate. The missing exact limits remain a project input, not a number Atlas should invent. Export/import symmetry must be checked at the largest valid created state and after metadata/schema changes.

## Decision worksheet

Answer these questions for each material state family; “unknown” is an explicit handoff gate:

1. What is authoritative, who may mutate it, and which values are only observations or drafts?
2. What survives route changes, reload, another tab, browser restart, sign-out or device loss? Which promises need independent recovery?
3. What exact event and candidate version permit success copy? What stays dirty if editing continues during a pending save?
4. What consistency boundary covers the operation? How are stale bases detected and reviewed without erasing newer work?
5. What happens on missing, denied, full, malformed, blocked or unsupported-version storage? Which actions may replace existing data?
6. What schema/growth envelope applies equally to created state and recovery? How do replacement, deletion and migration retire stale writers, queued saves and recovered drafts?

Choose the smallest mechanism that satisfies the answers. Choosing storage first and filling in these answers afterward tends to hide unresolved product decisions.

## Project handoff and validation

Put the resolved answers in the consuming project's self-contained `design.md`: state/owner table; draft and save boundaries; candidate/dirty-baseline and completion ordering; acknowledgement copy; persistence and loss limits; schema/capacity/version contract; conflict policy; recovery/reset/import/export flows and stale-writer retirement; dependencies; exact unresolved owner inputs; performed evidence and pending checks. Include concrete [focus/feedback and dirty-exit rules](forms-and-navigation.md#modal-editing-and-dirty-exit) when actions open dialogs or leave editors. Include authoritative remote-status recovery from [uncertain outcomes](uncertain-outcomes.md) when a request may outlive the page.

For Pocket Practice, schema bounds, history growth, conflict reapplication, backup format and browser baseline remain inputs. For Form & Field, cart concurrency/retention and an independent checkout-attempt recovery contract remain inputs; preserving a cart does not resolve an unknown purchase outcome.

**Desk-review scenarios, not executed tests:** trace save A followed by edit B and A completion; reset/import followed by a queued old save or stale-tab edit; reload during pending save; save abort/quota failure; denied startup access; unreadable and newer-version records; two tabs editing the same base; a new conflict during review; blocked/interrupted migration; full-size valid export/reimport; invalid or unsupported import; failed reset; explicit temporary mode followed by storage recovery; cleared storage followed by return. Each trace must identify visible state, preserved data, permitted next action and required evidence before success. Actual supported-browser, interruption, accessibility and service testing remain future implementation work.

# UI/UX design decisions

Status: adaptation draft, updated 2026-10-20. Original Atlas synthesis by **Tamir (Phi Vuong Tuong Tam), with Codex AI assistance**. No product validation is claimed.

## Load for a specific design question

Read when preparing or deliberately revising task, content, journey, or visual decisions. Select sections that resolve the brief. Keep identity, tokens, type choices, effects, and motion recipes in the theme package. Resolve selected decisions into the project's self-contained `design.md`; choose tools from that project's constraints.

## Frame the problem and evidence

Write who is trying to do what, in which situation, what prevents progress today, and what a useful outcome would be. Describe users by relevant behavior, knowledge, access, and context. Start with available research, observations, support reports, or an owner brief. Synthetic personas and invented quotations are not prerequisites.

Distinguish **observed evidence**, with source/date and limits; **binding constraints**, such as permissions or service contracts; and **hypotheses** awaiting a check. A stakeholder preference does not prove user need. With thin evidence, choose a reversible proposal, name the assumption, and identify what better evidence could change. Do not invent conversion targets or task times.

“Find an unfinished application and identify the next action” has an observable outcome; “an intuitive dashboard” leaves success unresolved.

## Tasks, content, and information structure

Name the primary task and necessary supporting tasks. Identify their entry points, required information, permitted actions, and observable completion. Include content people use to decide or compare: labels, dates, limitations, ownership, and next steps as relevant. Use realistic short, long, empty, and unavailable content.

Group information around user decisions. Establish consistent names for objects, actions, navigation, and destinations. Decide what belongs in the main path, supporting detail, search/filtering, or a later step. Reveal complexity when useful, while keeping material costs and consequences available before commitment. Record tradeoffs where compactness makes comparison harder or fewer steps remove useful explanation.

## Journeys across screens and time

Describe consequential transitions through current state, actor/trigger, prerequisites, next state, feedback, and available next action. Cover meaningful branches, backtracking, cancellation, and correction alongside success. Explain transitions and the effect on earlier choices.

Trace interruption and return: leaving a route, closing a tab, losing connectivity, following a deep link, or resuming after a delay. What can actually be restored? What changed or expired? What summary helps reorientation? What needs review? Promise continuity only where the project has an identified mechanism.

Load [state and recovery](state-and-recovery.md) for authority, retention, save acknowledgement, and durable drafts; [forms and navigation](forms-and-navigation.md) for validation, dirty exit, branching steps, focus, and resume; and [uncertain outcomes](uncertain-outcomes.md) when remote effects can outlive the screen or a missing reply makes retry unsafe. Those chapters own detailed contracts; the journey records where they affect the user task.

## Hierarchy, type, color, density, and words

Reuse the theme's visual language and the project's current component owners. Resolve these decisions for the selected surface:

| Concern | Question to answer with real content |
| --- | --- |
| Hierarchy | What should be noticed first, compared next, and acted on? Do grouping and reading order support the task? |
| Typography | Which existing roles carry titles, body, controls, and metadata? Do wrapping, fallback, and long values preserve meaning? |
| Color | Which semantic roles indicate action, status, and emphasis? Which rendered foreground/background pairs need measurement? |
| Density | Which information must stay visible together? Where can detail expand without hiding needed context or obscuring controls? |
| UX writing | Do labels predict results, instructions explain decisions at the point of need, and feedback state what is known and possible next? |

A different spacing value or typeface is not itself a usability failure. Tie departures to constraints, contradictions, or demonstrated task difficulty. Measure color pairs when needed; a palette image cannot establish rendered contrast. Load [focused accessibility and responsive decisions](accessibility-and-responsive.md) when input methods, assistive technology, content growth, or adaptation affect this task.

Motion is optional. Name its purpose, such as showing a relationship or confirming a transition, and consider repeated use and interruption. Preserve information and controls when motion is reduced or absent. Keep timings and recipes with the theme. When the project's motion mapping remains unresolved, use the [chosen motion contract](accessibility-and-responsive.md#record-the-chosen-motion-contract) to resolve the handoff.

## Translate the design through components

When component mapping is unresolved, trace the approved design role to its semantic token, existing component owner, relevant variant and visible state. Record an intentional exception. A matching hex value or component name alone does not establish that the implementation follows the contract.

Use a bounded specimen when it helps resolve the question: only used controls and compositions, realistic content, and consequential states beside the normal case. Label simulated states outside the control's real text. Keep fixture overrides local to the specimen. A pinned focus or hover appearance supports visual inspection; it does not demonstrate keyboard operation, focus transfer or assistive-technology behavior.

Resolve the accepted mapping into project-owned values or stable token references. Verify the relevant real interactions when implementation evidence is available; record missing checks. The sample is optional and need not become an exhaustive component showcase.

Method credit: **shadcn and contributors**, selected [design-system](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui/blob/ba1503c64472b82256d9de95e2e62c5901a38e8b/skills/shadcn/design-system.md) and [specimen guidance](https://github.com/shadcn-ui/ui/blob/ba1503c64472b82256d9de95e2e62c5901a38e8b/skills/shadcn/design-system-page.md) at `ba1503c64472b82256d9de95e2e62c5901a38e8b`, MIT, copyright 2023 shadcn. Preserve the [full notice](../references/licenses/shadcn-MIT.txt) with a distributed substantial adaptation. Atlas narrows the method to the existing project; it does not adopt upstream initialization, install-all or automatic stack-selection instructions. Third-party registry assets retain separate terms. See the [adaptation boundary](../references/skill-adaptations.md#2026-10-20-reference-and-craft-additions).

## Handoff and realistic validation

Record task/surface scope; evidence and assumptions; content/navigation model; important transitions; theme decisions and justified exceptions; dependencies and unresolved inputs; and performed versus pending checks. In existing interfaces, trace governing documents, components, variants, and tokens to the selected rendered surface before reporting drift. Similar names elsewhere do not prove ownership.

Choose representative tasks and likely failure conditions. A desk walkthrough asks whether a person can notice an action, predict its effect, recognize progress, recover, and resume; label its conclusions as hypotheses. When feasible, observe intended users attempting realistic tasks without coaching. Record context/sample limits, hesitations, errors, completion, and recovery. Small samples expose problems but do not establish population rates. Repeat affected tasks after changes. Identify which conclusions rely on source, screenshots, automated checks, or user observation.
